evals.name: notification-system-five-layers
evals.prompt: /hamburger-method We need to notify users when a product they're watching drops in price
evals.expected_output: Identifies 3-6 functional layers (not technical layers like frontend/backend/DB). Generates at least 4-5 options per layer following a manual→scripted→automated→scalable→enterprise quality gradient. Proposes a smallest vertical slice using level-1 or level-2 options from each layer. The smallest slice delivers end-to-end value and can be built in hours, not days. Proposes 2-3 follow-up slices.

assertions.text: Identifies functional layers (detect event, identify recipients, format message, deliver, track) NOT horizontal technical layers (frontend, backend, database)
Generates at least 4 distinct options for EACH layer — not just 'simple vs complex'
Options within each layer follow a quality gradient from manual/hardcoded to automated/scalable
The proposed smallest vertical slice uses level-1 or level-2 options (manual/scripted) — NOT level-4 or level-5 options
The smallest slice is end-to-end: covers all layers, even if at the lowest quality level
Proposes at least 2 follow-up slices that improve one or two layers incrementally

evals.name: search-feature-radical-slicing
evals.prompt: /hamburger-method Add a search feature to our e-commerce site so users can find products
evals.expected_output: Identifies layers for a search feature (input capture, query execution, result display, ranking/relevance, tracking). Forces radical slicing: smallest slice is a simple text filter on existing product list, not a full-text search engine. Options per layer go from hardcoded list to ML-powered ranking.

assertions.text: Identifies layers appropriate to search: input capture, query execution, result rendering, ranking, and tracking — or equivalent functional decomposition
Generates at least 4 distinct options per layer following the quality gradient
The smallest vertical slice does NOT require a search engine (Elasticsearch, Solr) — starts with simple string matching or a filtered list
Explicitly applies the 'ship by tomorrow' question to force radical slicing to the simplest possible option
The smallest slice is deployable and provides real user value, even if limited (e.g., basic text filter on product name)

evals.name: reporting-dashboard-multi-layer-options
evals.prompt: /hamburger-method Build a sales dashboard that shows monthly revenue, top products, and customer acquisition trends so our CEO can make decisions
evals.expected_output: Identifies 4-6 layers (data source, aggregation/computation, presentation/visualization, access/delivery, drill-down/interactivity). Generates 4-5 options per layer. Smallest slice delivers ONE useful metric to ONE user (the CEO) using the simplest possible stack. Defers interactivity and drill-down to later slices.

assertions.text: Identifies layers that cover data pipeline AND presentation concerns — not just 'show metrics'
Generates at least 4 distinct options per layer with explicit quality gradient
The smallest vertical slice delivers exactly ONE metric (not all three) to validate the concept before building more
Interactivity (drill-down, filters, custom date ranges) is deferred to a follow-up slice — NOT in the first slice
The smallest slice explicitly identifies who will use it (e.g., the CEO or one internal user) and what decision it enables
Uses the numbered option system (1.1, 1.2, 1.3... for layer 1; 2.1, 2.2... for layer 2) to label options

evals.name: resist-infrastructure-first-instinct
evals.prompt: /hamburger-method Implement a real-time chat feature between customers and support agents
evals.expected_output: Detects that 'real-time' triggers over-engineering instinct. Forces options that start without WebSockets/Kafka/Redis. Smallest slice is polling or even manual (support agent checks email). Proposes WebSockets only in a later slice. Challenges the assumption that 'real-time' must be the first slice.

assertions.text: Identifies functional layers for chat: message input, message delivery/routing, message display, history/persistence, presence/status
Generates at least 4 options per layer with quality gradient
The smallest vertical slice does NOT use WebSockets, Kafka, or Redis — uses polling, email, or manual checking instead
Explicitly challenges whether 'real-time' is needed for the first slice — asks 'can we validate the core value without real-time infrastructure?'
Includes at least one 'manual/crutch' option per layer — e.g., support agent checks an email inbox instead of a realtime dashboard
The smallest slice is designed to validate the core user value (customer gets help) before investing in real-time infrastructure

evals.name: authentication-flow-hard
evals.prompt: /hamburger-method Implement user authentication with SSO, MFA, social login (Google and GitHub), and session management for our SaaS application
evals.expected_output: Detects multiple 'and' signals but does NOT just say 'split it' (that's story-splitting territory). Instead applies hamburger layers to the authentication domain. Identifies layers: identity verification, credential storage, session management, MFA enforcement, social provider integration. Smallest slice is username/password only with no MFA, no social login. SSO and MFA are later slices. Generates 4-5 options per layer.

assertions.text: Does NOT just split into separate stories — applies layered options to each authentication concern
Identifies functional authentication layers: identity verification, credential storage, session management, MFA, social providers
Generates at least 4 options per layer with explicit quality gradient

The smallest vertical slice covers exactly ONE authentication method end-to-end — SSO, MFA, and multiple providers are explicitly deferred to follow-up slices (starting with OAuth-only or password-only are both valid)
SSO integration is identified as a high-complexity option and deferred beyond the first 2 slices
The smallest slice is production-deployable and provides real value (users can actually log in), not just a prototype
Proposes at least 4 follow-up slices showing the incremental path from basic auth to full SSO+MFA

evals.name: ml-recommendation-engine-hard
evals.prompt: /hamburger-method Build a product recommendation engine that uses machine learning to suggest relevant items to users based on their browsing and purchase history
evals.expected_output: Detects that 'machine learning' and 'browsing and purchase history' are high-complexity signals. Applies hamburger method to show that ML is NOT required in the first slice. Layers: data collection, model/algorithm, candidate generation, ranking/filtering, presentation. Smallest slice uses hardcoded rules or simple popularity-based recommendations. ML is explicitly a level-4 or level-5 option. Forces the question: 'can we validate that recommendations increase sales without ML first?'

assertions.text: The smallest vertical slice does NOT use machine learning — uses hardcoded rules, popularity ranking, or manual curation instead
Machine learning appears as a level-4 or level-5 option within the algorithm/model layer — not as the starting point
Identifies layers appropriate to recommendations: data collection, algorithm, candidate selection, ranking, presentation
Generates at least 4 options per layer with explicit quality gradient
Explicitly asks whether the business value (increased sales/engagement) can be validated with a simple rule-based approach before investing in ML infrastructure
The smallest slice can realistically be shipped within 1-2 days — not weeks — and produces visible recommendations to users
Data collection is identified as a separate layer/concern — NOT bundled into 'we need ML data first'

evals.name: already-small-no-hamburger-needed
evals.prompt: /hamburger-method Add a 'copy to clipboard' button to the API key display on the settings page
evals.expected_output: Recognizes this feature is already small (< 1 day). Does NOT apply hamburger layers — there is nothing to slice. Does NOT generate 4-5 implementation options per layer for something trivial. Explicitly confirms this is appropriately sized and can be implemented directly.

assertions.text: Identifies the feature as small (a few hours at most) and does not require hamburger method decomposition
Does NOT produce a multi-layer table with 4-5 options per layer — avoids over-engineering a trivial UI interaction
Explicitly recommends implementing it directly without the hamburger method process
Does NOT add 'slices', 'layers', or incremental rollout plans to a feature that is already a single-session implementation

grading_guide.capability_assertions: The output explicitly demonstrates the described reasoning or produces the stated content. Evidence must be present in the response, not inferred from context.
grading_guide.behavior_assertions: The output does or avoids the described action. Binary: did it happen or not.
grading_guide.layer_quality: To count as a pass on functional-layer assertions, layers must represent business/functional steps (detect → notify → deliver) NOT technical tiers (frontend → backend → DB). Naming a layer 'Backend' or 'Database' is a fail.
grading_guide.options_quality: To count as a pass on 'four-options-per-layer' assertions, each option must be concretely named (e.g., '1.1: hardcoded list', '1.2: keyword filter') — vague descriptions like 'simple version' or 'advanced version' do not count.
grading_guide.slice_quality: The smallest vertical slice must be end-to-end (covers all layers) and use only level-1/2 options. A slice that skips layers or requires new infrastructure (queues, ML models, WebSockets) in the first iteration is a fail.
grading_guide.false_positive_calibration: Eval 7 is the false-positive check. A pass requires the skill to NOT apply the hamburger method AND to explicitly confirm the feature is small enough to implement directly. Producing layers for a trivial feature is a fail.
grading_guide.skill_vs_model_delta: The key question for skill justification: does the skill force the model to generate ALL layers AND ALL options (not just describe the concept), and does it reliably prevent the over-engineering instinct for the 'hard' cases (evals 4, 5, 6)? If the base model produces equivalent output without the skill, the skill adds no value.
grading_guide.statistical_requirements: With min_runs=3, report mean, stddev, min, max per metric. A delta is only meaningful if confidence intervals do not overlap.
